hook.text: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy containing 200 to 400 billion stars. We live about two-thirds of the way out.

buildup.text: It spans 100,000 light-years across. Our solar system sits in the Orion Arm, a minor spiral arm.

discovery.text: The Sun orbits the galactic center at 828,000 km/h. One full orbit takes about 230 million years.

twist.text: We can't photograph the Milky Way from outside. Every image you've seen is an artist's interpretation or another galaxy.

climax.text: Mapping our galaxy is like mapping a city while standing on one street corner. Dust blocks most of the view.

punchline.text: We live inside it but can't see its shape. Home is the hardest place to map.

quiz.question: Why can't we photograph the Milky Way from the outside?
options: We are inside it, and interstellar dust blocks much of the view
The Milky Way is invisible to all types of telescopes
Light from the Milky Way is too dim to capture

details.summary: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across, containing 100-400 billion stars, a supermassive black hole at its center, and our solar system roughly two-thirds from the center in the Orion Arm.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding our home galaxy provides the framework for all of astronomy. The Milky Way's structure, dynamics, and history shape the environment in which our solar system formed and our Sun orbits.
takeaways: A barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across
Contains 100-400 billion stars and a central black hole
Our solar system sits in the Orion Arm

faq.question: Can we see the Milky Way from the outside?
faq.answer: Not from our current position — we're inside it. Our understanding of its structure comes from mapping star positions (the Gaia satellite has mapped nearly 2 billion), radio observations of gas, and comparing it to similar external galaxies.

faq.question: How long does it take to orbit the galaxy?
faq.answer: The Sun orbits the galactic center at about 230 km/s, taking roughly 225-250 million years to complete one orbit — a 'galactic year.' The Sun has completed about 20 orbits since the solar system formed 4.6 billion years ago. Stars at different radii orbit at different speeds.
